title: Murle Age-Sets, Warriors and Social Organization
subtitle: The history, order and social importance of the Murle buul from Longoroket to Guzulee
author: Murle Connect

body.heading: The Murle Buul: A Society Organized by Generations
paragraphs: Among the Murle people, the age-set system, known as buul, is one of the most important institutions of social life. An age-set is a named generation whose members develop a shared identity, responsibilities and relationships that can continue throughout their lives.

The buul system is not simply a method of calculating a person's age. It organizes relationships between generations and helps determine patterns of cooperation, authority, responsibility, marriage relationships, community protection and social support.

Every Murle man normally belongs to an age-set. Age-set identity remains important even when a person leaves the rural areas, moves to Pibor town or Juba, or lives in the diaspora. The institution therefore connects Murle people across different places and circumstances.

The age-set system works together with the clan and drumship system and the institution of the red chiefs. These institutions are different from one another, but together they form an important part of traditional Murle social organization.

body.heading: The Order of the Murle Generations
paragraphs: Murle age-sets are traditionally understood through seniority. Older generations are followed by younger generations, and each new generation eventually becomes the younger generation in relation to those that follow it.

The broad historical sequence documented in written sources can be presented from the oldest to the youngest as: Longoroket, Nyakademo, Nyerza, Maara, Dorongwa, Muden, Titi, Butotnya, Lango, Kurenen and Guzulee.

The spelling of several names differs between sources. For example, Nyakademo may appear as Nyakedemo or Nyakademu; Nyerza as Nyeriza; Titi as Thithi; Butotnya as Bothonya, Bothoth or Bothothniya; and Lango as Lanngo or Laŋo.

The age-set system is also not a permanent list. New generations emerge over time, while older generations eventually disappear. For this reason, the list represents the historical development of the Murle generations rather than a fixed list that can never change.

Older historical documentation records Longoroket as the oldest generation in this sequence. More recent Murle Heritage documentation records Guzulee as the youngest age-set under formation, following Kurenen.

body.heading: 1. LONGOROKET
paragraphs: Longoroket is recorded in historical documentation as the oldest generation in the extended Murle age-set sequence.

The generation is associated with people born around the first decade of the twentieth century and the years immediately after it. By the time modern researchers documented the Murle age-set system, only a very small number of Longoroket members were still alive.

The importance of Longoroket is therefore not only the age of its members but also the historical memory carried by that generation. Its members belonged to a Murle society that existed before many of the political, administrative, military and technological changes that later transformed the region.

Historical accounts also describe Longoroket as the generation whose disappearance opened the way for the formation of a new younger generation. This illustrates an important principle of the traditional system: the relationship between generations is continuous, with younger generations eventually replacing older generations in social prominence.
Because Longoroket belongs to the early twentieth-century historical record, information about it is more limited than information about younger age-sets.

body.heading: 2. NYAKADEMO
paragraphs: Nyakademo, also written Nyakedemo or Nyakademu in different sources, followed Longoroket in the older documented sequence.

The generation is broadly associated with people born during the 1910s and 1920s. By the period in which modern researchers documented the Murle age-set system, very few members of Nyakademo remained.

Members of this generation grew up during a period when colonial administration was becoming increasingly established in the region. Their lives were still deeply connected to cattle, agriculture, local communities, traditional leadership, age-set relationships and movement across Murle territory.
Nyakademo represents one of the generations through which knowledge of early twentieth-century Murle society was transmitted to younger generations.

body.heading: 3. NYERZA
paragraphs: Nyerza, also written Nyeriza, is the generation that followed Nyakademo. It is broadly associated with people born during the 1920s and 1930s.

The generation lived through the later colonial period and the transition toward Sudanese independence. Its members therefore experienced major changes in administration, education, trade, religion, communication and relations with government authorities.
Nyerza is also important because its members became elders during the period when Sudanese national politics and the First Sudanese Civil War began to affect southern Sudan more directly.
The generation became part of the older advisory structure of Murle communities as younger generations emerged beneath it.

body.heading: 4. MAARA
paragraphs: Maara, (Mara), followed Nyerza and is broadly associated with people born during the 1930s and 1940s.
Members of Maara experienced the final period of Anglo-Egyptian administration in Sudan, Sudanese independence in 1956 and the beginning of the First Sudanese Civil War.

The generation therefore lived through the transition from colonial rule to independent Sudan. This was a period in which government administration, taxation, armed conflict and new political structures increasingly affected communities in the south.
Maara members gradually moved into senior positions within their communities as younger generations assumed the responsibilities traditionally associated with youth.
Historical documentation associates the lion with Maara in the Murle age-set tradition, although age-set symbols and their interpretation can vary across sources and communities.

body.heading: 5. DORONGWA
paragraphs: Dorongwa, (Doroŋwa or Dorong), followed Maara and is broadly associated with people born during the 1940s and 1950s.

Dorongwa is particularly important in modern Murle history because the late Ismael Konyi belonged to this generation. Konyi became a major traditional, military and political figure in the history of the Pibor region.
Members of Dorongwa experienced the First Sudanese Civil War, the period following the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972 and the beginning of the Second Sudanese Civil War.
The generation therefore grew up during a period in which traditional Murle social structures increasingly interacted with national armed movements and changing political authorities.
Dorongwa members later became elders and senior advisers, while younger generations took over many of the physical responsibilities associated with youth.

body.heading: 6. MUDEN
paragraphs: Muden, (Moden or Mudech) in different forms, followed Dorongwa and is broadly associated with people born during the 1950s and 1960s.

Muden came of age during a period of increasing political instability and armed conflict in Sudan. Members of the generation were affected by the Second Sudanese Civil War and by the growth of armed organizations in the Pibor region.
Historical sources record that members of Muden joined forces associated with Ismael Konyi and the Pibor Defence Forces during the later twentieth century.

The experience of Muden illustrates how the traditional age-set system could become connected to modern armed movements without being identical to those movements. An age-set was a social generation; a military organization was a political and military formation.
Muden is associated with the giant pouched rat in Murle age-set symbolism in contemporary heritage documentation.

body.heading: 7. THITI
paragraphs: Titi, (Thithi or Thithoch), followed Muden and is broadly associated with people born during the 1960s and 1970s.
The generation came of age during the Second Sudanese Civil War and experienced some of the most important political and military transformations in southern Sudan.

Members of Titi were involved in different political and military environments. Some became associated with the Pibor Defence Forces, while others became involved with the Sudan People's Liberation Army and later political structures.
Titi therefore represents a generation that experienced both traditional Murle social organization and the increasing influence of national armed movements.
The blue-capped cordon-bleu is associated with Titi in Murle age-set symbolism, with green and blue commonly associated with its identity.
As Titi members grew older, many moved into the roles of elders, advisers and community leaders.

body.heading: 8. BOTHONYA
paragraphs: Bothonya (Bothoth). It followed Titi and is broadly associated with people born from the late 1970s through the 1980s and into the early 1990s.

Bothonya became one of the most important generations in the modern history of Murle age-set competition. Historical sources describe it as the first Murle age-set associated with the transition from traditional stick fighting between competing young generations toward the use of firearms in age-set conflict.
The generation came of age during the final period of the Second Sudanese Civil War and the years surrounding the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005.

Members of Bothonya were involved in the political and military transformations that affected Murle society during the early twenty-first century. David Yau Yau, one of the best-known political and military figures connected to the Murle community, belonged to this generation.

Bothonya also became closely connected with the emergence of new forms of age-set identity and competition. Body markings began increasingly to include symbols of modernity and military power rather than only traditional animal imagery.

The knob-billed duck is associated with Bothonya in Murle Heritage documentation, while other contemporary sources describe different animal and visual associations. This reflects the fact that age-set symbolism can change over time and may vary between communities.

body.heading: 9. LANGO
paragraphs: Lango, (Laŋo or Lanngo), followed Bothonya and is broadly associated with people born during the 1980s and 1990s, with some sources describing the generation as extending into the early 2000s.
Lango became a major social generation in the period surrounding the end of the Second Sudanese Civil War and the emergence of South Sudan as an independent country.

The generation became prominent during a period of rapid political, social and military change. Many Lango members experienced displacement, armed conflict, cattle-based livelihoods, urban migration and the expansion of communication technologies.

Lango became involved in competition with both the older Bothonya and the younger Kurenen generation. These relationships demonstrate that age-set competition was not simply a question of age but also involved social status, marriage, cattle, authority and control over community responsibilities.
The antelope or kob is associated with Lango in Murle Heritage documentation. Yellow and black are commonly associated with its beads.

Modern research has also documented the development of nyakenet or ken sub-groups within age-sets, particularly among younger generations. These groups can develop their own names, dances, songs, bead arrangements and body markings.

body.heading: 10. KURENEN
paragraphs: Kurenen is the generation that followed Lango. It is broadly associated with people born from the mid-to-late 1990s onward.

Older research described Kurenen as an emerging generation. More recent Murle Heritage documentation now identifies it as an established younger age-set, while Guzulee is described as the age-set under formation beneath it.

Kurenen members grew up during the period of South Sudan's independence and the conflicts that followed independence. Their childhood and youth have therefore been shaped by a mixture of traditional Murle life, modern education, mobile phones, social media, towns and continuing rural livelihoods.

The gazelle or deer is associated with Kurenen in Murle age-set descriptions. Contemporary research also records white, brown and other colours associated with Kurenen beads, with exact colour combinations varying between sources and groups.

Kurenen demonstrates how Murle age-set identity continues to adapt. Younger people can maintain traditional ideas of generation and belonging while also incorporating symbols and experiences from the modern world.

body.heading: 11. GUZULEE
paragraphs: Guzulee is the youngest generation in the contemporary Murle age-set sequence documented by Murle Heritage.
It is associated broadly with people born during the 2000s. Murle Heritage describes Guzulee as an age-set under formation and approaching a future separation from Kurenen.

Because Guzulee is the newest generation, its social identity is still developing. Its members are growing up in an environment very different from that of Longoroket, Nyakademo or even the older twentieth-century generations.

Guzulee members are experiencing Murle life alongside smartphones, social media, formal education, modern political institutions, migration, urban life and the continuing importance of cattle and traditional community relationships.

The spotted guineafowl is associated with Guzulee in Murle Heritage documentation. The use of a token animal continues the older Murle tradition of connecting each generation with an animal whose characteristics become part of its identity.
Guzulee represents the continuing nature of the Murle generation system. The system does not end with the older generations; it continues to produce new identities as new generations come of age.

body.heading: The Age-Sets Are Not Fixed Birth-Year Categories
paragraphs: It is important not to treat Murle age-sets as exact ten-year birth brackets in the same way that a modern census classifies people by year of birth.

Research generally describes Murle age-sets as groups loosely based on age, with approximately ten-year intervals in some periods. However, the boundaries have not always been identical, and the timing of the emergence of a new age-set can vary.

Historical evidence shows that the younger age-set can emerge only after particular social conditions are met. Older documentation from Pibor describes the death of the oldest generation as an important condition for opening a new age-set.

The formation of new age-sets can also take years and can spread between different parts of Murle territory at different speeds. Highland and lowland Murle communities have not always experienced the emergence of new age-sets at exactly the same time.
For this reason, the birth periods given in this article should be understood as approximate historical ranges rather than strict boundaries.

body.heading: Age-Set Membership Is Lifelong
paragraphs: A defining feature of the Murle buul is that membership normally lasts throughout a person's life.
Murle boys generally enter an age-set as they reach the stage of social maturity and are normally expected to remain associated with that generation.

There are exceptions. Historical and contemporary accounts describe situations in which people can move between age-sets or receive honorary membership in another age-set. Such movement can occur because of family circumstances, political considerations or the death of an older brother who carried particular responsibilities.
These exceptions demonstrate that the system is not mechanically determined by birth year. Social responsibilities and relationships also matter.

body.heading: Brothers and Fathers Do Not Simply Belong to the Same Generation
paragraphs: Murle age-set organization creates relationships between generations within the same family. Brothers can belong to different age-sets, and a son does not simply enter the same age-set as his father.
This arrangement allows families to maintain relationships across several generations. Different brothers can therefore provide representation and connections across different age-set groups.
The system creates a social structure in which age-set relationships cross family relationships. A person's loyalty and responsibilities are therefore shaped both by ancestry and by generation.

body.heading: Age-Set Alliances Across Generations
paragraphs: Murle age-sets do not exist as completely isolated generations. Relationships can develop between particular age-sets across the generational order.

Murle Heritage documents relationships between every second age-set in which one generation may be connected to the generation that corresponds roughly to its father's age-set. For example, Kurenen has been described as aligned with Bothonya, while Lango has been described as aligned with Thithi.
These relationships create another layer of organization within Murle society and help explain why age-set relationships cannot be understood simply as older people versus younger people.
The strength of these relationships has also changed over time, particularly as political and military conditions have changed.

body.heading: Age-Sets and Marriage
paragraphs: Age-set organization has historically influenced marriage relationships and the timing of marriage among Murle youth.
Younger generations traditionally waited for older generations to move through important stages of marriage and family formation before fully entering the same social competition.
This created a system in which age-set seniority was connected to the social availability of marriage, cattle and bridewealth.

Changes in cattle ownership, warfare, displacement, education, urbanization and modern employment have changed many aspects of this system, but age-set identity continues to influence relationships and social expectations.

body.heading: Age-Sets and Warrior Responsibilities
paragraphs: Young Murle men have traditionally had responsibilities connected with cattle, community protection, movement, hunting, labour and defence. The age-set provided a structure through which these responsibilities could be organized.

This is why age-sets are sometimes described simply as warrior groups. That description is incomplete. An age-set is a social generation first; warrior responsibilities are only one part of its wider role.

Historically, young men could participate in controlled contests and stick fighting as part of the relationship between generations. Older generations and traditional authorities could help regulate these competitions.

During the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, firearms and prolonged civil conflict changed the character of some age-set competition. Researchers have documented the movement from earlier forms of stick fighting toward more dangerous armed confrontations among some younger generations.
It is therefore important to distinguish the traditional social institution of buul from modern armed groups. An age-set is not itself a political party, army or militia.

body.heading: From Traditional Symbols to Modern Symbols
paragraphs: Murle age-sets have historically used animals, colours, beads, songs, dances and body markings to express their identity.
Older generations commonly used natural animals and birds as important age-set symbols. Members associated themselves with the qualities and appearance of their selected animal.

Researchers have documented an important change among younger generations. From the period around the 2000s onward, body markings increasingly incorporated symbols associated with modernity, education, weapons, military organizations, phones, writing and political institutions.

This change does not mean that traditional symbols disappeared. Instead, new symbols were added to an older cultural practice. The body became a place where young Murle people could express both traditional generation identity and their experience of the modern world.

body.heading: Nyakenet: Sub-Groups Within the Younger Generations
paragraphs: Modern research has documented the development of smaller groups within some Murle age-sets. These are known as nyakenet, with nyakeno sometimes used for the singular form.
A nyakenet may consist of close friends or younger members within an age-set. In recent decades, these groups have developed their own names, songs, dances, bead arrangements and body markings.
The development of nyakenet has added another layer to Murle social organization. Instead of having only one identity as an age-set, some young people also identify strongly with their smaller group.
Researchers have linked the growth of these sub-groups to the effects of conflict, militarization, urbanization and changing ideas of modernity.

body.heading: Age-Sets and the Clan System
paragraphs: The age-set system is not the same thing as the Murle clan system.
Murle society has four major clans or drumships: Taŋajon, ŋarɔti, Keleŋnya and ŋenvac. Clan identity is based on ancestry and descent, while age-set identity is based primarily on generation.
A person therefore has an ancestral position through the clan system and a generational position through the buul system.

The two systems cross one another and help connect Murle communities. People from different clans can belong to the same age-set, creating social relationships that extend beyond immediate family and ancestry.

body.heading: Age-Sets, Red Chiefs and Authority
paragraphs: Each Murle age-set has traditionally been connected to red chiefs, known as alan ci merik. These chiefs come from the red-chief lineages associated with the Murle drumship system.
The relationship between age-sets and red chiefs is important because Murle society does not operate through one centralized king or a single chain of command.
Age-set authority, clan authority, red-chief authority, elders and local community leadership overlap and interact. Their responsibilities can vary according to place, generation and circumstances.
Traditional authorities have historically helped regulate disputes between age-sets and maintain relationships between younger and older generations.

body.heading: Boma and Pibor: One People, Different Experiences
paragraphs: The Murle age-set system exists across the Murle homeland, but its expression can differ between the Boma highlands and the Pibor lowlands.

Environmental conditions have shaped differences in livelihood, settlement, cattle movement and community organization. These differences have sometimes affected how age-set membership and seniority operate.

Historical research has shown that an age-set may become established in the lowlands before it becomes established in Boma. This is one reason why an age-set's history should not automatically be assumed to have developed in exactly the same way in every Murle community.
These differences do not mean that Boma Murle and Pibor Murle are separate peoples. The age-set system remains one of the institutions connecting Murle communities across their different landscapes.

body.heading: The Age-Sets During Sudan's Civil Wars
paragraphs: The generations of the twentieth century experienced Sudan's First and Second Civil Wars in different ways.
Older generations such as Maara, Dorongwa and Muden experienced the transition from colonial administration to independent Sudan and later the growth of armed conflict.

Titi, Butotnya and Lango came of age during increasingly militarized periods. Members of these generations became involved in different armed and political organizations, including forces associated with the Sudan People's Liberation Army and the Pibor Defence Forces.
The historical record shows that age-set structures were sometimes used to mobilize young men, but the age-set system itself was older than these military organizations and cannot be reduced to them.

body.heading: The Age-Sets After South Sudan's Independence
paragraphs: South Sudan became independent in 2011, but the Murle age-set system continued to operate.

Younger generations grew up during a period characterized by political instability, conflict, displacement, education, mobile communication and increasing movement between rural communities and towns.
The younger generations therefore inherited the traditional buul system while also living in a very different social environment from the generations before them.
This produced changes in age-set identity, including new sub-groups, new symbols and new forms of communication. At the same time, the basic principle of belonging to a generation remained strong.

body.heading: The Generational Chain
paragraphs: The complete historical sequence preserved in this article is: Longoroket, Nyakademo, Nyerza, Maara, Dorongwa, Muden, Titi, Butotnya, Lango, Kurenen and Guzulee.
Each generation inherited a Murle society shaped by the generations before it. At the same time, each generation changed the society it inherited.

Longoroket belongs to the early twentieth-century historical memory. Nyakademo and Nyerza carried that memory through the colonial period. Maara and Dorongwa experienced independence and war. Muden and Titi lived through major civil-war transformations. Butotnya and Lango came of age during the transition toward peace and later conflict. Kurenen and Guzulee are growing up in the era of independent South Sudan, digital communication and rapid social change.
The sequence therefore provides a way of reading modern Murle history through generations.

body.heading: The Meaning of Buul Today
paragraphs: The Murle buul remains one of the strongest forms of social identity among Murle people.

A person can live far from the Murle homeland and still identify with an age-set. Age-set identity can remain relevant in family relationships, friendships, community organization, political networks, social support and cultural activities.

At the same time, the system is changing. Education, Christianity, Islam, government institutions, urbanization, migration, modern employment, technology and conflict have all affected the way younger generations experience the traditional system.
The survival of the buul therefore does not mean that Murle society has remained unchanged. Instead, it demonstrates how an old institution can adapt to new historical circumstances.

body.heading: Why the Age-Set History Matters
paragraphs: Understanding the Murle age-set system is essential for understanding Murle history itself.

The generations provide a framework for remembering who lived through different periods, how responsibilities moved from elders to youth, how traditional authority operated and how Murle society responded to colonial rule, Sudanese independence, civil wars and the creation of South Sudan.

The buul also shows that Murle identity is not based on one institution alone. Clan, family, age-set, community, language, land, cattle, traditions and historical memory all contribute to the identity of the Murle people.
Preserving the names of the generations is therefore an important part of preserving Murle history.

historicalNote: Murle age-set names, spellings, approximate birth periods and the timing of new generations vary across sources and communities. This article combines an older historical record that documents Longoroket through Lango with newer Murle Heritage documentation that includes Kurenen and Guzulee. Longoroket is therefore retained as a historical generation rather than treated as a currently active age-set. The sequence should not be interpreted as a rigid birth-year classification. Murle age-sets are social generations whose formation, membership and seniority can change over time and may develop differently in different parts of Murle territory.
